questions.stem: Shipper declares `String quote(Object parcel)`. ExpressShipper extends Shipper and declares `String quote(Parcel parcel)`. A checkout runs `Shipper shipper = new ExpressShipper(); shipper.quote(new Parcel("P-17"));`. Which method runs?

options.text: ExpressShipper's quote(Parcel), since the method is chosen when the call runs, and the object and argument are an ExpressShipper and a Parcel
options.says: the compiler chooses the overload from declared types; only the override of the chosen method is picked at run time

options.text: ExpressShipper's quote(Parcel), since quote(Parcel) takes a narrower parameter, and so it replaces the parent's quote(Object)
options.says: a different parameter list makes it an overload, not an override, as equals(Sku) did not override equals(Object)

options.text: Shipper's quote(Object), since the compiler chose it from Shipper's methods, and quote(Parcel) doesn't override it
options.says: the variable is declared Shipper, whose only quote takes an Object; quote(Parcel) is a separate overload, so no override of quote(Object) exists

options.text: Shipper's quote(Object), since the variable is declared as Shipper, and a parent-typed variable runs the parent's version
options.says: an override in the subclass would run through a parent-typed variable; here there is none

origin.section: The Compiler Chooses an Overload From the Arguments' Declared Types

questions.stem: A billing class has `charge(double amount)` and `charge(Long cents)`. A caller writes `long cents = 1999; charge(cents);`. What happens?

options.text: charge(Long) runs, since boxing a long to Long is tried in an earlier phase than widening it to double
options.says: widening is allowed in the first phase and boxing only in the second, the reverse of this order

options.text: charge(Long) runs, since among the overloads that fit, the compiler picks the one whose type is closest to long
options.says: there is no closeness measure; the first phase already found charge(double), and boxing is never tried

options.text: charge(double) runs, since widening a long to double is tried in an earlier phase than boxing it to Long
options.says: widening is allowed in the first phase, boxing only in the second, and the first phase that finds a candidate wins

options.text: charge(double) runs, since among the overloads that fit, the compiler picks the one whose type is widest
options.says: within a phase the most specific overload wins, not the widest; here only one overload fits in the first phase

origin.section: Widening First, Then Boxing, Then Varargs: the First Phase That Fits Wins

questions.stem: Version 1 of a notification library has `send(Object payload)` and `send(String text)`, and an app calls `send(null)` to clear a banner. Version 2 adds `send(byte[] raw)`. The app's build is updated to version 2. What happens to the call?

options.text: It compiles and calls send(Object), since neither String nor byte[] is a subtype of the other
options.says: there is no fallback to a common supertype: when no candidate is the most specific, the call is ambiguous and doesn't compile

options.text: It compiles and calls send(Object), since String and byte[] are both subtypes of Object
options.says: null goes to the most specific overload, never to Object as a fallback; here none is the most specific, so the call doesn't compile

options.text: It fails to compile, since neither String nor byte[] is a subtype of the other
options.says: two candidates where neither type is a subtype of the other make the call ambiguous, as audit(String) and audit(Integer) did

options.text: It fails to compile, since String and byte[] are both subtypes of Object
options.says: being subtypes of Object makes String and byte[] more specific than send(Object), not ambiguous with it, as audit(String) beat audit(Object); the clash is between String and byte[]

origin.section: null Goes to the Most Specific Overload, and Two Unrelated Ones Don't Compile

questions.stem: A reporting class declares `void export(List<Order> orders)` and `void export(List<Refund> refunds)`, where Order and Refund are unrelated classes. What does the compiler do with the class?

options.text: It accepts it, since the parameter types differ in their type arguments, which the call's declared list type selects between
options.says: type arguments are erased from the signature, so both methods have the same erased parameter types and clash

options.text: It accepts it, since the parameter types differ in their type arguments, which the list's elements select between at run time
options.says: overloads are never chosen at run time, and these two don't compile in the first place

options.text: It rejects it, since the two methods have the same name, and the same parameter types once type arguments are dropped
options.says: both erase to export(List): a name clash, as total(List<Integer>) and total(List<Double>) showed

options.text: It rejects it, since the two methods have the same name, and the same return type while their type arguments differ
options.says: the return type never distinguishes overloads, since it isn't part of the signature; the type arguments, erased, are what make the two clash

origin.section: Overloads Must Differ in Erased Parameter Types: the Return Type and Type Arguments Don't Count
